proxy_language: Proto-Sino-Tibetan (Old Chinese-style reconstruction, Baxter-Sagart 2014) as a speculative north-China proxy, with Proto-Yeniseian and Proto-Mongolic only as areal cross-checks
proxy_rationale: Shuidonggou (c. 30-10 ka) and Xiachuan (c. 24-16 ka) are known only from lithics, hearths and fauna; no linguistic affiliation is demonstrable and the languages of these hunter-gatherers are almost certainly extinct without descendants. The only defensible choice is a regional proxy: Old Chinese (as reconstructed by Baxter-Sagart 2014) and Proto-Sino-Tibetan as the best-documented deep language family of the Yellow River region. This link is purely geographic; a 20,000-year gap makes any real genetic connection unprovable, and the microblade tradition may equally relate to Siberian/Yeniseian or Altaic-area populations. Names should therefore sound plausibly northern East Asian without claiming attestation.
phonology: Old Chinese (Baxter-Sagart 2014 notation, simplified): stops and affricates in three-way manner (plain *p *t *k, aspirated *ph *th *kh, voiced *b *d *g), nasals *m *n *ng, fricatives *s *h, liquids *r *l, glides *w *j, labiovelar *kw *khw *gw, glottal stop; vowels *a *i *u *e *o *ə (Baxter-Sagart use six vowels *a *i *u *e *o *ə). Codas: *-p *-t *-k *-m *-n *-ng *-r *-w *-j, plus *-ʔ and *-s suffix traces. Proto-Sino-Tibetan roots are typically monosyllabic CV(C) with sesquisyllabic prefixed forms (s-, r-, m-, b-, g-, d-). No tone in the reconstruction; for game use, tone is not marked.
phonotactics: Main syllable: (C)(C)V(C) with a single vowel nucleus; onset clusters limited to prefix + root (s-, m-, r-, k-, p- before stops/sonorants) or stop+liquid/glide (pr-, kr-, kl-, kw-); codas one consonant, from p t k m n ng r w j. No vowel hiatus; no word-initial ng- in most proxy forms (allowed in Old Chinese, avoid for readability). Words mostly monosyllabic roots, names built as 1-3 syllables (compounds of 2 roots typical). Never finish a root with b d g or h in written form.
orthography: Latin transliteration with plain letters: p t k b d g m n ng s h l r w y a e i o u, plus ə written as e for game purposes. Use 'y' for the palatal glide, 'ng' as a digraph, 'kh' 'th' 'ph' for aspirates. No diacritics, no q, no c, no f, no v, no z, no x. Hyphen may link two components of a compound. Reconstructed forms in sources carry asterisks; game names do not.
morphology: Isolating-analytic with residual prefixes and suffixes. Sino-Tibetan roots: noun and verb roots are monosyllabic and uninflected; derivational prefixes s- (causative/transitive, animate), m-/b- (nominaliser, agent), r-/d-, g- (body parts, stative), and suffixes -s (nominaliser/derivational), -ʔ. No case, no gender, no number marking on nouns; plurality by numerals, collective particles or reduplication. Verbs unmarked for tense.
compounding: Compounds are head-final: modifier + head (Old Chinese attributive pattern, e.g. mountain-god = 'mountain' + 'god'). Genitive 'X of Y' is rendered Y-possessor + head (possessor first), optionally with the particle *tjə (zhī) in Old Chinese; for the proxy write possessor + head directly, e.g. 'sun house' for 'house of the sun'. Agent nouns 'Y-maker' are verb-object order reversed to object + verb root + agent nominaliser (e.g. stone strike person); in game names use object + action root, with optional nominaliser s-/m- on the second element. Names are typically two roots joined with a space or hyphen.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier before head: adjective/noun/possessor/demonstrative + noun; numerals and classifiers before the noun. Relative clauses before the noun. 'Big river' = big + river; 'River of the horse' = horse + river.

worked_examples.name: Suy rak
worked_examples.gloss: suy 'water, river' + rak 'cook, boil' (modifier + head, noun-verb compound)

worked_examples.name: Kok sak
worked_examples.gloss: kok 'stone' + sak 'flake, cut' (object + verb root, agent reading)

worked_examples.name: Taj ran mu
worked_examples.gloss: taj 'great' + ran 'mountain' + mu 'spirit, god' (modifier + modifier + head)

sources: Baxter, William H. and Laurent Sagart. Old Chinese: A New Reconstruction. Oxford University Press, 2014.
Matisoff, James A. Handbook of Proto-Tibeto-Burman. University of California Press, 2003.
Wiktionary: Reconstruction:Proto-Sino-Tibetan and Old Chinese reconstruction appendices (Baxter-Sagart)
Gao Xing, Zhang Xiaoling et al. on Shuidonggou site excavations (archaeological context only)
Norman, Jerry. Chinese. Cambridge University Press, 1988.
notes: This is a deliberately speculative proxy. No language of the Shuidonggou or Xiachuan hunter-gatherers is known, and Pleistocene languages of north China left no demonstrable descendants. Forms above are Old Chinese/Proto-Sino-Tibetan-flavoured models for sound shape, not claimed words of the culture; reconstructed items are marked and glosses should be treated as approximate. Several 'roots' are simplified and should be used only as phonological templates. No game name may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since this culture's language is not Goidelic; check generated names against those lexicons and reject any exact match.
unit: North China late Palaeolithic microblade groups (Shuidonggou, Xiachuan)
